en: Their voices made souls depart.
With pinewood spears bound together,
In the lowlands of Jelpinish,
For seven years we waged unceasing war.
In conflict I could not overcome them;
In struggle my strength did not suffice.
For six months I traveled without rest,
Sparing no horse, traveling far.
My preserved provisions ran out,
I came eating my saddle straps.
My nest-mate, Khan Manas,
I came hoping he would give me an army.
With Almambet and Chubak at its head,
I came hoping he would give generously.
Ajybai and Bakai, the paired warriors,
I came hoping he would give me both.
Syrgak and Sergek, ocean-like warriors,
I came hoping he would give them all.
Wearing out my horse, to the courser,
I came hoping for help.
To my auspicious kinsman Manas,
Who kindles an extinguished fire,
Who restores a dead soul to life—
I am bending beneath my burden;
I came hoping he would support me.
Restoring a dead soul to life,
I came hoping he would sustain me.
When it flies toward the sunrise,
A bird's wings grow weary.
After crossing the threshold,
To return and visit one's birth family
Is a woman's custom.
Elder Bakai, surpassing lion,
Support me when I bend!
I have suffered much oppression from Kökdöö.
Elder Bakai, sustain me!
Kindle the extinguished fire,
Restore the dead soul to life!
You were leopard Bakai;
The one who went on watch and fought
Was I, unfortunate Kardygach.”
Then Bakai said this,
Told horrors no mortal should see:
“I shall tell my story, Kardygach.
It has been twelve years
Since your khan elder Bakai died;
Twelve full years have passed.
Deeply has my pit been dug,
God has boiled my bitter sorrow.
Hear the tale, my child Kardygach!
My great black cap, broad as a cauldron,
Has become grass—you have come at such a time.
My suffering exceeds my fortune—
You have come at such a time.
The torments of the grave, stretched out gaunt,
You have come when I am about to see it.
My chest has begun to rattle,
My eyes have filled with pus.
You have come when I am dying!
Semetey came to my side;
You appeared when my lot improved.
All the chosen fierce warriors
Had vanished when you appeared.
Khan Bakai, neither dead nor gone,
Was crawling when you appeared.
In these days, Khan Bakai—
His valor gone, he is no warrior,
And great Bakai, wearing his shroud,
Is not rotting in the earth either.
My child Kardygach, hear my words!
While your bloodthirsty Manas lived,
Into great Beijing, looming dark,
When we entered straight and thrust our spears,
From hell with its grievous torment,
When we freed our souls,
Of Beijing, which Solomon could not touch,
When we returned having taken its rule,
Beijing, which Alexander could not touch,
When we returned having made it serve us,
Into Beijing, which the Flood could not reach,
When we returned having thrown it into turmoil,
Its gold and silver,
When we hauled more than we could load,
Noble wives and beautiful girls,
When we returned, unable to seize them all,
Entering Beijing and taking its emblems,
Facing Beijing and taking its land,
Those high-born men who deemed themselves valiant,
Taking many a lion from Beijing,
The golden-doored gates,
Bringing down governors and taking palaces,
With shoes of gold,
Taking amblers no horse could match,
Leaving silver and taking gold coins,
With slender legs and roomy dresses,
Taking the mincing Chinese girls,
Upon mist-covered Beijing,
Turning back after laying it waste,
Turning and fighting for six months,
Losing our coursers.
In those days, until the supple stalks ripened,
Until the autumn gossamer flew,
We thrust our spears firmly,
Fought without rest for six months.
Entering the khakan's realm and returning,
We saw days of ruin,
Losing our leopards.
In the seething clashes,
In the crashing battles,
Earth flew, stones burned,
On the march where we endured hell.
Earth fell and blood flowed
In the tumultuous battle.
Of Beijing, the city blessed by Khizir,
Scouting its cliff paths and returning,
Great Bakai had seen such deeds,
Losing his champions.
Of hell-like Beijing,
As they made the toorumak shots,
Great affliction, enduring hell,
Losing those as mighty as mountains.
When the hellish battle raged,
Muzburchak and Khan Kökchö died.
All who encountered Beijing died.
Kökötöi's Bokmurun,
The warrior, his only son, died.
Messengers died, khans died;
All who traveled to the khakan died.
The road Khizir had traversed died;
All who went to Beijing died.
Noble Manas, the generous lion,
There brought accursed days upon Bakai.
On the ridge of that great Beijing,
Akkula was shot down,
Almambet passed away a martyr.
Fighting and turning back,
The one we looked to for support,
Khan Chubak, we lost.
The foreign Chinese and many Manchus,
Driving them apart and returning,
He had just reached twenty—
We lost warrior Syrgak.
Warrior Serek died in combat;
Warrior Bozuul died as well.
The laughing lion Küldür died;
Twelve mighty lords among the companions died.
Going on watch and scouting,
The generous warrior was praying,
And was speared beside the spinal cord.
My generous Khan Manas died.
And I go on, Kardygach,
Herding camels and grieving,
Bereft of my lords.
Wanting to die, unable to die,
Unable to take my own life,
We saw a night no daylight cleared.
My goatskin coat upon my body,
My hide trousers upon my ass,
My child, my camel calf, Kardygach,
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Such is this world of shit.
In those days, when your elder brother Manas died,
The countless riches your brother left,
Abyke, Köbösh—the six scoundrels—
Divided by measuring with a whip.
Then Kanykei departed in mourning;
Semetey fled away.
Plundering fine cloth, they prospered,
Semetey entered Bukhara and grew up.
In those days, Kanykei left a widow,
Semetey left an orphan.
His lot improved each day.
He entered Bukhara and grew up,
Matured and became a warrior,
The equal of grown warriors.
My spring flowing from the hills,
This boy with whom you have been fighting
Is your lamp left by generous Manas.
Ah, Kardygach, my foal!
You have troubled my thoughts.
You turned and pursued
The child left by the courser.
My life had become a dark cliff.
Joining the six scoundrels,
All forty pigs became enemies.
The forty were dogs from forty places.
If not dogs, what sort of men were they?”
Grief-stricken, poor Kardygach,
When it heard this,
Her black hair, untouched by a comb,
She tore out in strands and cast away.
Losing her senses, she screamed.
The wretched one sobbed, “Ah, my nest-mate!
I went to a place beyond sight,
And did not see you, ill-fated me!
Now, my falcon Manas, take me with you!
Handfuls upon handfuls of silk strands,
I did not grasp and tear from every side.
Coming from the land of the sunset,
My kinsman, I did not see you.
While you strode about in wrath,
Did I slice and eat horse-belly fat?
Coming suddenly with the news,
Did you mean to make me lament?”
Unfortunate Kardygach said this.
Upon her smooth white face
She set her five nails,
And tore again and again.
As she tore, dark blood flowed;
Kardygach's strength departed.
Her tears streamed thinly.
Blood flowing from both cheeks
Poured down past her collarbones.
Kardygach screamed and wept.
When she heard the truth about Manas,
Her voice reached God.
From upon Telküröng,
She rolled and fell.
As Kardygach was thus,
Honored Khan Bakai wept;
The ill-fated orphan wept too.
The birches wept, the willows wept;
All who looked on wept.
Kardygach tried to take courage.
Khan Bakai spoke words of courage:
“Ah, Kardygach, my foal,
Among horses, the sleek bay has passed away.
The father of all these people,
Father Adam himself has passed away.
Many mighty warriors have passed,
Many different peoples have passed,
Many powerful giants have passed.
Wailing will not bring back the departed;
Grieving will not restore those who have gone.
This one you have been pursuing
Is your elder brother, bloodthirsty Khan Manas's,
Only son, whom he looked to for support.
My child Kardygach, hear my words.
In those days, at Kökötöi's memorial feast,
Infidel and Muslim
Had gathered in great numbers.
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan,
Who joined hands with twelve as one,
The saintly elder Koshoi,
Of the market that lay bound,
The elder who opened its fortune,
Of the sorrowful one in bonds,
The elder who untied his hands,
Whose blessing enriched the people,
Whose regard brought brightness to a life,
His white beard flowing,
Making his gray ambler sway,
Raised in a sacred land,
Raised among people who kept their word,
When he spoke, his words were clear,
A true saint, a seer.
